title: 3-Read Friday #32: Mini Whiteboards, Mind-Wandering, and CPD
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #32 covers mini-whiteboard routine design, research on mind-wandering, and a warning about ineffective CPD. Barton praises Mason Davies's granular walkthrough of a whiteboard routine, including question design and a closing FAQ section, calling himself 'a sucker for a post about mini-whiteboards.' He highlights Andrew Watson's research deep-dive into student mind-wandering as having results that are 'scary (but maybe unsurprising)' with 'profound' classroom implications. He then endorses Adam Robbins's argument that most CPD fails to produce lasting change, revealing that Barton has started requiring headteachers to sign a 'charter' before he'll support their maths department -- a commitment shaped directly by Robbins's argument.
points: Barton calls himself 'a sucker for a post about mini-whiteboards' and praises Davies for walking through every step of his routine, including question design and a closing FAQ section.
He frames Watson's mind-wandering research summary as having 'profound' classroom implications, despite results that are 'scary (but maybe unsurprising).'
He reveals that Robbins's CPD critique directly shaped his own professional practice -- he now requires headteachers to sign a 'charter' before he'll support their maths department.
quotes: You know by now that I am a sucker for a post about mini-whiteboards, and this one by Mason is really nice.
He takes us through every step of his routine, including how he designs his questions, providing justifications for each step.
Andrew takes one of his customary deep dives into a piece of research - this time on a recent study into the prevalence and impact of student mind-wandering.
The results are scary (but maybe unsurprising), and the implications for the classroom are profound.
In the next few weeks, I will write a newsletter about a charter I now get all Headteachers to sign up to before I agree to support their maths department.
The reason is precisely as Adam points out in this post - if we are not careful, most CPD will have little long-term benefit.
